title: Sidewalk & delivery robots (PDD laws)
summary: States set operating rules for personal delivery devices, while local governments may consider additional requirements. Pennsylvania’s statute treats qualifying devices as pedestrians under specified conditions; a Philadelphia fee remains a proposal.
key_points: Pennsylvania Act 106 of 2020 establishes rules for qualifying personal delivery devices, including operation and insurance requirements.
Philadelphia Bill 260526 proposes a $1,000 fee per sidewalk delivery by an autonomous unit; the city lists it in committee as of October 26, 2026.
State rules differ in speed, weight, insurance and pedestrian-yield requirements.

title: Autonomous vehicles & robotaxis
summary: State permitting rules govern autonomous-vehicle testing and deployment alongside federal vehicle safety requirements. California distinguishes drivered testing, driverless testing and deployment; passenger service has separate CPUC oversight.
key_points: California DMV adopted updated rules in April 2026 allowing manufacturers to apply to test and deploy heavy-duty autonomous vehicles, subject to permits and safety requirements.
DMV lists approved locations and conditions for testing and deployment permits; a testing permit alone does not authorize passenger service.
California’s CPUC regulates autonomous passenger service through separate programs and permits.

title: Incentives, R&D credits & site selection
summary: States use broad jobs, investment, and research incentives that robotics firms may qualify for. Program thresholds matter: a large Texas facility and a small Michigan research shop face different eligibility tests.
key_points: Texas Enterprise Fund is a performance-based cash grant, not a robotics tax credit; it requires a competing out-of-state site and significant jobs and investment.
Michigan’s general refundable R&D credit began with 2025 tax years; New York’s Excelsior program lists manufacturing, R&D, and software eligibility with job thresholds.
Pennsylvania created Innovate in PA 2.0 with up to $125 million, dependent on tax-credit sales; California Competes lists its next application windows in January and March 2027.
State records and source links appear below on this States page; confirm current application and tax rules with the administering agency.

title: Robotics clusters & workforce pipelines
summary: Robotics networks in Pennsylvania and Massachusetts connect companies, researchers and training programs. Their offerings illustrate local talent and commercialization infrastructure without ranking the clusters.
key_points: The Pittsburgh Robotics Network connects the region’s robotics organizations.
MassRobotics offers the Jumpstart fellowship for Massachusetts high-school students, with training and paid internship opportunities.
MassRobotics also runs challenges and startup programs with industry partners.

title: State AI laws × autonomous systems & federal preemption
summary: State automated-decision laws can affect some AI uses, but ordinary robot operation is not automatically covered. Colorado changed its law in 2026; its new ADMT Act applies to consequential decisions starting January 1, 2027. The White House March 2026 framework proposes federal preemption in some areas, but Congress has not enacted that proposal.
key_points: Colorado SB 26-189 governs automated technology that materially influences covered consequential decisions; its effective date is January 1, 2027.
Colorado’s Attorney General filed proposed rules in August 2026 and scheduled a public rulemaking hearing for October 26; comments may continue if the hearing continues.
The March 2026 White House AI framework is legislative advice to Congress, not itself a change in state authority.
For any robot use case, check whether its AI makes a covered decision, then check applicable state and local law.
